bodyMarkdown:
## Before you start

Coordinate reading, and proportion.

## The idea in plain language

A bubble chart squeezes three numbers into one picture. Left-to-right is one variable, up-and-down is a second, and the **size** of the bubble is a third.

So a bubble far right, high up and large is scoring well on all three — and a question asking 'which is best' usually needs you to say which of the three you are judging on.

## What is actually going on

Read the two axes first, then check what the legend says bubble size encodes. Size is the dimension people forget.

Be careful comparing bubble sizes by eye: a bubble that looks twice as wide has four times the area, so visual comparison badly exaggerates differences. Where exact values matter, the question will normally give them in a table alongside.

## Every question type you will meet

Each of these is a shape a question in this topic actually comes in. Learn to recognise the shape first — in a timed paper, picking the right method is most of the battle, and the arithmetic is the easy part.

### 1. Reading three variables at once

**Spot it when:** plotted circles of differing sizes.

1. The x and y positions are two variables; the bubble's size is a third.
2. Read position from the axes and size from the legend.
3. Do not infer the third variable from position — they are independent.

**Worked through:** A bubble far right and low may still be the largest by the third variable.

### 2. Ranking by the size variable

**Spot it when:** 'which had the greatest sales', where sales is the bubble size.

1. Use the size legend rather than judging by eye.
2. Bubble size is usually scaled by **area**, so a circle that looks twice as wide represents about four times the value.

**Worked through:** Doubling the radius quadruples the area, so it represents four times the quantity.

## Check yourself

You are ready to start practising this topic when you can:

- Read all three variables off a bubble chart.
- Use the legend rather than eyeballing size.
- Explain why apparent width overstates differences.

workedExamples.stemMarkdown: Bubbles plot revenue on the x-axis, profit margin on the y-axis, and headcount as size. A firm is far right but low down with a small bubble. Describe it.
workedExamples.solutionMarkdown:
Far right means high revenue.

Low down means a low profit margin.

A small bubble means few employees.

So it is a high-revenue, low-margin business run by a small team.

formulaCards.title: Three variables at once
formulaCards.bodyMarkdown: x-position, y-position, and bubble size are three separate readings. Always check the legend for what size means.
formulaCards.exampleMarkdown: Two bubbles at the same height differ only in the x-variable and in size.

commonTraps: Comparing bubble sizes by width when area is what encodes the value.
Ignoring the size dimension entirely and treating the chart as a scatter plot.
Assuming position implies causation between the two axis variables.
